content_html:
I would like to thank Microsoft product teams and Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) for collaborating with me on this technical analysis and mitigation of the disclosed vulnerabilities. The editorial opinions reflected below are solely the author’s and do not necessarily reflect those of the organizations I collaborated with.

Summary

The findings described in this post are part of a coordinated disclosure with MSRC and Microsoft product teams. Microsoft was provided with reproduction steps, videos, environmental assumptions, and the exact proof-of-concept (PoC) prompts used during testing. They were also informed of a 90-day coordination period before disclosure. This was extended two times, resulting a 144-day coordination period.

In parts 1 and 2 in this series, I have shown how external inputs could influence Copilot responses and, in some cases, potentially lead to confidentiality impacts through Cross-Domain Prompt Injection Attacks (XPIAs). This report builds on those findings and extends the XPIA analysis from single-interaction compromise to propagation across trusted document workflows. It shows that attacker-controlled instructions in one document can be copied into Copilot-generated or Copilot-edited Word documents, causing those downstream documents to become new carriers of the same attack.

Previous examples of AI-worms exist. Notably, Morris II demonstrated self-replicating prompt propagation in GenAI-powered email-assistant ecosystems. However, to my knowledge, this is among the first public demonstrations of document-borne AI-worm self-propagation through normal workflows in a mainstream commercial productivity suite.

The reported scenario is:

  1. Malicious instructions hidden in an externally shared document could make Copilot alter drafted or edited documents in Word and propagate the attack to new documents.

The full attack in brief

The attack

An attacker places hidden instructions in a document that is later used as source material in Copilot for Word. Copilot may interpret those instructions as part of the user’s request, causing it to manipulate the document being drafted or edited. Copilot may then also copy the hidden instructions into the resulting document, turning that document into a new carrier. If the carrier is subsequently used in another Copilot-assisted workflow, the instructions can trigger again and propagate into further documents, even without the attacker’s original document being present.

Example

Consider an employee preparing a financial report. The employee downloads a market analysis from a trusted website that has been compromised, unaware that the document contains hidden instructions. The employee then includes the analysis as source material when drafting the report with Copilot. The hidden instructions cause Copilot to alter internal figures in the financial report and copy the attack into the new document. The employee saves and shares the apparently legitimate report internally. Later, a colleague uses it as source material for another report; the instructions trigger again, alter the new report, and copy themselves forward. The attack can therefore continue without further involvement from either the compromised website or the original malicious document. As affected reports are reused, additional reports and documents can become carriers of the attack.

Disclosure status at publication

  • Vendor: Microsoft
  • Coordinated disclosure: Handled through MSRC and Microsoft product teams
  • Included in this post: XPIA and self-propagation scenario in Microsoft Copilot for Word
  • Customer action: No customer-side remediation fully addresses the issue at the time of publication. Customers can reduce exposure by:
    1. Treating externally sourced documents as untrusted when used with Copilot.
    2. Reviewing any attached document before starting a Copilot generation or edit.
    3. Carefully reviewing Copilot-generated or Copilot-edited documents before reusing, sharing, or distributing them.
  • Microsoft-side status: Testing has reproduced the attack with all current mitigations deployed. At the time of publication, no robust mitigation for the broader vulnerability class is available.

A note on disclosing before a fix

Unlike Parts 1 and 2, this scenario remains exploitable at publication. I have weighed that carefully. The coordination period agreed with Microsoft has been exhausted, and testing shows that no robust mitigation for the broader vulnerability class is currently available. Two mitigation attempts, including a model upgrade, did not close the class.

I have therefore chosen to disclose at the class level rather than the payload level. My reasoning is that defenders cannot reduce exposure to a risk they are unaware of, and the propagation mechanism described here affects ordinary document workflows that many organizations already rely on. Withholding the existence of the issue would leave those organizations unable to make an informed decision, while providing no additional protection.

Disclosure timeline

  • 2026-03-06: Initial report submitted to MSRC with reproduction steps, videos, environmental assumptions, and PoC prompts.
  • 2026-03-09: MSRC acknowledged receipt and opened a case.
  • 2026-03-31: Microsoft confirms the reported behavior.
  • 2026-03-31: Microsoft product teams began mitigation work; ongoing technical discussion.
  • 2026-04-03: First mitigation go-live (The new “Edit with Copilot” experience)
  • 2026-04-09: Original attack prompt wording verified mitigated with “Edit with Copilot”.
  • 2026-04-09: Attack behavior reproduced in “Edit with Copilot” using a new XPIA prompt task (manipulating financials). Reported as separate case to MSRC.
  • 2026-04-10: MSRC acknowledged receipt and opened a case.
  • 2026-04-10: Microsoft product teams began mitigation work; ongoing technical discussion.
  • 2026-06-08: At Microsoft’s request, public disclosure was moved to 2026-07-15.
  • 2026-07-14: Second mitigation fix go-live. This mitigation consisted of upgrading the underlying model to GPT-5.5.
  • 2026-07-15: Successful exploit with worming reproduced using GPT-5.6, the latest available model at the time.
  • 2026-07-15: I suggest we postpone disclosure a further two weeks to 2026-07-28, to allow time for a new mitigation.
  • 2026-07-15: Microsoft agreed.
  • 2026-07-28: Attack still reproduces.
  • 2026-07-28: Coordinated public disclosure (this post).

Threat model

The attacker does not need access to the victim’s Microsoft 365 tenant. The attacker only needs to share a malicious document with the victim. This can be done through SharePoint, Teams, Outlook or any other way of sharing documents.

Security boundary and observed behavior

The relevant security boundary in this scenario is the boundary between attached documents and the current drafting document. If any of the attached documents contain an XPIA the attack may trigger.

Copilot must read every attached document to determine which parts to include in its current drafting task. However, attached documents should be treated as untrusted information, not trusted user instruction.

Boundary violation
Attacker-controlled documents are downloaded or shared through email/sharepoint/other sharing option. If such documents are attached to Copilot during a drafting task, trust is broken.

Expected behavior
When a user asks Copilot to draft e.g. a Q1 financial report based on attached documents, Copilot should utilize the information in the attached documents without treating instructions embedded within documents as authoritative instructions.

Observed behavior
Instructions embedded in documents cause Copilot to alter its behavior. Here presented as:
1: Copilot silently changing numerical values in financial reports
2: Copilot propagating the full XPIA by pasting into downstream documents, which may then be used as attachments in later drafting sessions\

Crossing the trust boundary in Word

The initial attack vector for these scenarios uses a malicious document. The malicious document contains a JSON-formatted malicious prompt that triggers the attack when the document is included in Copilot’s context. The prompt can be rendered as white text on a white background and in a small font size to conceal it from the victim. Since Copilot for Word strips all text formatting like color and font size before passing the text into the underlying Large Language Model (LLM), this text remains fully readable to Copilot even though the victim cannot see it. The attack can be further concealed by embedding it in a seemingly benign document with task-relevant text.

This attack requires the malicious document to be included as part of Copilot’s context in Word. Thus, depending on the version of Copilot in use, the victim must either:

  1. Actively attach or upload the document in Copilot for Word.
  2. Use the “Edit with Copilot” functionality in work/Work IQ mode and let Copilot find the malicious document in the victim’s OneDrive. In this case, Copilot must deem the document relevant and include it in the context. An attacker therefore needs to craft a document that increases the likelihood of either or both.

The exploit is relevant both for the “magic pen” and the “Edit with Copilot” functionalities in Word.

The attack happens in two stages. The first stage establishes foothold and in the second stage the attack self-propagates across documents that use Copilot for Word as part of drafting or editing.

Stage 1:

In the first stage the attacker has crafted a document that contains a malicious hidden prompt. In my initial PoC I used a document that only contained the malicious prompt as white text on white background. This was done to illustrate that the malicious document did not need to be relevant to the victim’s task for Copilot to use it. If it was included in the context, it is read and therefore the attack may trigger.

The PoC prompt was structured in two parts:

  • The first part contained the instructions on how to affect a document. This could range from slightly changing meanings of summaries to altering numbers in financial documents. The key was formulating the prompt in a way that made Copilot believe it was task-relevant and benign. In many of my experiments I actually needed to also instruct Copilot to highlight which changes it made, since they were often meaningful changes that were difficult to spot. This shows how effective the attack is at subtly changing the text in meaningful ways that easily elude even an attentive reviewer. In a real-world setting, the attacker would obviously not include such instructions. For the rest of this disclosure, therefore, I’ll use altering numbers in financial reports since that is an immediately visible change.

  • The second part contained the instructions to self-propagate the attack. The exact wording also matters here, but it was generally framed as serving the purpose of tracking sources in downstream documents. It also contained instructions on how to hide itself, framed as instructions to improve readability.

Figure 1: The initial attack vector document. I created a full mock company named Tfosorcim Ltd. for this PoC, with mock economics and vision. This attack vector document is a fake market analysis made using information about the company that would typically be available to an attacker. The attack is appended at the end of the document using white text. [Most of the XPIA text is blurred for security]

Once this malicious document was included in the context when drafting or editing a document with Copilot for Word, the attack would trigger and Copilot would execute the instructions. Thus, the affected document would have financial numbers changed. Copilot would then also copy the entire malicious prompt into the bottom of the affected document using white text and font size 8, effectively concealing it from the victim.

Figure 2: The downstream draft generated by Copilot used my malicious document as an attachment ([att] Direct wmr.docx). In the resulting Q1 financial report draft, all financial numbers are halved. The screenshot also shows other attached documents (Tfosorcim internal documents).

Figure 3: The figure demonstrates that GPT-5.6, the latest model from OpenAI at the time of writing, was used in these PoCs.

Figure 4: After having halved all financial numbers in the Q1 financial report draft, Copilot also appends the full attack prompt using white text to effectively conceal it from the victim. It also makes no mention about its halving of numbers or that it includes the attack. Thus, the victim is clueless of it. [Most of the XPIA text is blurred for security]

Figure 5: Copilot does not require the victim to attach the malicious document though. In this screenshot the victim only instructs Copilot to write a Tfosorcim Q1 financial report. Copilot then searches through the victim’s OneDrive to find relevant documents. Among the documents, we find the malicious Market Analysis document. This document does not reside in the same folder as the rest of the Tfosorcim document. However, Copilot still finds it, reads it and is successfully exploited.

Stage 2:

Stage two is the self-propagation stage. It relies entirely on the instruction for Copilot to copy the malicious prompt into the affected document. Once the affected document contained the prompt, the new document itself became the new attack vector.

Figure 6: The screenshot shows a new drafting session using Copilot. This time the original attack vector is no longer included among the attachments. However, the previously created document is (Tfosorcim Q1 2026 report.docx). The result is the same, and Copilot again halves all financial numbers in the drafted Q2 financial report.

Figure 7: In addition to halving all financial numbers, Copilot adds the full attack prompt, again using white text. Thus, the attack propagates through Word documents, effectively creating a document-borne AI worm. [Most of the XPIA text is blurred for security].

Of note, this new attack vector is now an internally created document, with all the trust that follows. Thus, the victim needs only share this document with coworkers for the attack to spread. If the victim or a colleague then uses the affected document as an attachment to Copilot for Word while drafting or editing, the attack spreads to these new documents.

In all reported PoC scenarios, Copilot would alter generated or edited documents and copy the hidden instruction into these documents. When these documents were themselves used as part of the context for new downstream documents, the attack triggered again. Note that for the second phase, the original attack document was no longer part of the attachments for the new downstream documents, yet the attack triggered and spread to these as well.

Impact

Since the attack is able to spread through internal documents, once it has moved beyond its initial point of entry, the traceability of the attack becomes extremely difficult. This is further exacerbated by each document being created by a legitimate internal resource and that Copilot edits are not made visible after they have been approved by the victim. The broader concern is that, if the attack silently spread within an organization through ordinary document workflows, it could erode the informational foundation on which organizations make decisions.

In addition, organizations that are not aware that they are affected by the attack are also likely to spread it to other organizations through collaborative efforts on shared Microsoft SharePoint sites or shared Microsoft Teams. Thus, the initial attack vector for a particular organization may actually come from an already affected trusted partner. This again increases likelihood of the victim choosing to include the affected document in the Copilot for Word context during drafting.

Recently Copilot is also becoming more deeply integrated with systems such as Microsoft Cowork or Microsoft Scout, which extend the assistant to automatic manipulation and creation of documents, tools, and collaborative workflows. In such systems the practical impact of the issues described here may scale rapidly. The underlying mechanism remains the same, but the potential surface over which it can propagate or influence expands at machine speed.

Mitigating the vulnerabilities

Microsoft successfully mitigated the originally submitted PoC prompt, and deployed multiple fixes over the course of this disclosure. Each of these raised the bar by closing the specific payloads reported, and reproducing the behavior afterwards required altered payloads rather than reusing the old ones directly.

The original report, however, also described the broader vulnerability class, in which instructions embedded in a source document could influence Copilot’s generation and copy themselves into downstream documents. Changing the requested action or wording changes the payload, but not the underlying vulnerability or propagation mechanism. Using a modified payload, the complete attack chain has been reproduced with all mitigations deployed (the PoC in this report is one such case). The vulnerability class therefore remains exploitable at the time of publication.

That the class is not yet fully closed reflects how hard the underlying problem is. As the closing thoughts discuss, the weakness is architectural and shared across current LLM-based systems. I’m not aware of a complete mitigation for this class in any comparable product today. Fully resolving it requires research rather than a single patch. Within those limits, Microsoft’s fixes meaningfully reduce exposure, and the memory and email-body vectors covered in Parts 1 and 2 were mitigated outright. I would like to thank Microsoft for their continued and substantive effort on a genuinely difficult problem.

Implications

Taken together with the two previous parts in this series, these findings point to a broader issue in modern work environments. Namely that the integrity of information becomes a primary security concern in systems that integrate LLMs as part of their operating workflows. The scenarios presented show that attacker-controlled content can not only influence individual outputs and potentially leak information. The attacks themselves can also be replicated and self-propagate through normal user workflows.

This introduces challenges that extend well beyond initial exploitation. Once malicious instructions are embedded in generated content, they may persist across documents, be redistributed by legitimate users, and be reintroduced into new contexts. At that point, the attack is no longer dependent on its original entry point. It has instead become part of the system’s internal information flow.

A related implication is the loss of traceability. Since affected content is generated and modified through legitimate workflows, the origin of the manipulation becomes difficult to identify after the fact. This complicates both detection and response, particularly in environments where such content is widely shared.

Independently of prompt-injection prevention, generated documents should preserve provenance for source material and model-performed edits in metadata. Such controls would not prevent the underlying injection, but they could make traceability much easier.

Closing thoughts

The findings in this series point beyond any single product or implementation. They expose a broader architectural weakness in current LLM-based systems.

For AI-assistants to be useful, they often must process emails, documents, webpages, memories, tool outputs, and other information that may be controlled by an attacker. To process that information, it must be included in the model’s context window, where it participates in the same computation as system instructions, user requests, and other trusted information.

This creates a fundamental problem: the LLM must process external content to determine what it means, whether it is relevant, and whether it contains an attack. But by the time it makes that determination, the attacker-controlled tokens are already influencing the computation that produces it. The content being inspected participates in the act of inspection. Relying on the model to detect XPIAs therefore resembles asking an interpreter to execute an untrusted program to determine whether that program is safe to execute.

Detecting and removing malicious content before it reaches the target model merely moves the same problem outward.

Because LLMs can recover semantics across radically different representations, an effective detector must possess comparable semantic recovery capabilities. A detector weaker than the target LLM will cover a smaller representational space, leaving malicious formulations that the target understands but the detector fails to recognize.

The only generally available technology with comparable semantic capabilities is another LLM. Placing one model in front of another may reduce the success rate of particular attacks, but it creates an “LLMs all the way down” problem, where every LLM introduced to protect another LLM must itself be protected.

The long-term challenge likely lies in designing systems in which goals and intentions also exist independently of the information being processed. Current LLM architectures provide no reliable separation between intention and interpretation. Thus, in current systems with embedded LLMs, attacker-controlled information can influence not only what the model produces, but what the model believes it has been asked to produce.

For that reason, any system that integrates an LLM into a trusted workflow today must assume that attacker-controlled content entering the model’s context will result in compromise at some rate.

The vulnerability class therefore remains exploitable at the time of publication.That the class is not yet fully closed reflects how hard the underlying problem is. As the closing thoughts discuss, the weakness is architectural and shared across current LLM-based systems. I’m not aware of a complete mitigation for this class in any comparable product today. Fully resolving it requires research rather than a single patch. Within those limits, Microsoft’s fixes meaningfully reduce exposure, and the memory and email-body vectors covered in Parts 1 and 2 were mitigated outright. I would like to thank Microsoft for their continued and substantive effort on a genuinely difficult problem.ImplicationsTaken together with the two previous parts in this series, these findings point to a broader issue in modern work environments. Namely that the integrity of information becomes a primary security concern in systems that integrate LLMs as part of their operating workflows. The scenarios presented show that attacker-controlled content can not only influence individual outputs and potentially leak information. The attacks themselves can also be replicated and self-propagate through normal user workflows.This introduces challenges that extend well beyond initial exploitation. Once malicious instructions are embedded in generated content, they may persist across documents, be redistributed by legitimate users, and be reintroduced into new contexts. At that point, the attack is no longer dependent on its original entry point. It has instead become part of the system’s internal information flow.A related implication is the loss of traceability. Since affected content is generated and modified through legitimate workflows, the origin of the manipulation becomes difficult to identify after the fact. This complicates both detection and response, particularly in environments where such content is widely shared.Independently of prompt-injection prevention, generated documents should preserve provenance for source material and model-performed edits in metadata. Such controls would not prevent the underlying injection, but they could make traceability much easier.Closing thoughtsThe findings in this series point beyond any single product or implementation. They expose a broader architectural weakness in current LLM-based systems.For AI-assistants to be useful, they often must process emails, documents, webpages, memories, tool outputs, and other information that may be controlled by an attacker. To process that information, it must be included in the model’s context window, where it participates in the same computation as system instructions, user requests, and other trusted information.This creates a fundamental problem: the LLM must process external content to determine what it means, whether it is relevant, and whether it contains an attack. But by the time it makes that determination, the attacker-controlled tokens are already influencing the computation that produces it. The content being inspected participates in the act of inspection. Relying on the model to detect XPIAs therefore resembles asking an interpreter to execute an untrusted program to determine whether that program is safe to execute.Detecting and removing malicious content before it reaches the target model merely moves the same problem outward.Because LLMs can recover semantics across radically different representations, an effective detector must possess comparable semantic recovery capabilities. A detector weaker than the target LLM will cover a smaller representational space, leaving malicious formulations that the target understands but the detector fails to recognize.The only generally available technology with comparable semantic capabilities is another LLM. Placing one model in front of another may reduce the success rate of particular attacks, but it creates an “LLMs all the way down” problem, where every LLM introduced to protect another LLM must itself be protected.The long-term challenge likely lies in designing systems in which goals and intentions also exist independently of the information being processed. Current LLM architectures provide no reliable separation between intention and interpretation. Thus, in current systems with embedded LLMs, attacker-controlled information can influence not only what the model produces, but what the model believes it has been asked to produce.For that reason, any system that integrates an LLM into a trusted workflow today must assume that attacker-controlled content entering the model’s context will result in compromise at some rate.Change LogThe following is a change log that shows which part of this post have been changed and at what time. blocks.html_en: An attacker places hidden instructions in a document that is later used as source material in Copilot for Word. Copilot may interpret those instructions as part of the user’s request, causing it to manipulate the document being drafted or edited. Copilot may then also copy the hidden instructions into the resulting document, turning that document into a new carrier. If the carrier is subsequently used in another Copilot-assisted workflow, the instructions can trigger again and propagate into further documents, even without the attacker’s original document being present.

blocks.html_en: Example

sentences.en: Example
sentences.zh: 例子

blocks.html_en: Consider an employee preparing a financial report. The employee downloads a market analysis from a trusted website that has been compromised, unaware that the document contains hidden instructions. The employee then includes the analysis as source material when drafting the report with Copilot. The hidden instructions cause Copilot to alter internal figures in the financial report and copy the attack into the new document. The employee saves and shares the apparently legitimate report internally. Later, a colleague uses it as source material for another report; the instructions trigger again, alter the new report, and copy themselves forward. The attack can therefore continue without further involvement from either the compromised website or the original malicious document. As affected reports are reused, additional reports and documents can become carriers of the attack.

blocks.html_en: The initial attack vector for these scenarios uses a malicious document. The malicious document contains a JSON-formatted malicious prompt that triggers the attack when the document is included in Copilot’s context. The prompt can be rendered as white text on a white background and in a small font size to conceal it from the victim. Since Copilot for Word strips all text formatting like color and font size before passing the text into the underlying Large Language Model (LLM), this text remains fully readable to Copilot even though the victim cannot see it. The attack can be further concealed by embedding it in a seemingly benign document with task-relevant text.

blocks.html_en: • The first part contained the instructions on how to affect a document. This could range from slightly changing meanings of summaries to altering numbers in financial documents. The key was formulating the prompt in a way that made Copilot believe it was task-relevant and benign. In many of my experiments I actually needed to also instruct Copilot to highlight which changes it made, since they were often meaningful changes that were difficult to spot. This shows how effective the attack is at subtly changing the text in meaningful ways that easily elude even an attentive reviewer. In a real-world setting, the attacker would obviously not include such instructions. For the rest of this disclosure, therefore, I’ll use altering numbers in financial reports since that is an immediately visible change.

sentences.en: Mitigating the vulnerabilities

blocks.html_en: Implications

sentences.en: Implications
sentences.zh: 影响

blocks.html_en: Taken together with the two previous parts in this series, these findings point to a broader issue in modern work environments. Namely that the integrity of information becomes a primary security concern in systems that integrate LLMs as part of their operating workflows. The scenarios presented show that attacker-controlled content can not only influence individual outputs and potentially leak information. The attacks themselves can also be replicated and self-propagate through normal user workflows.

sentences.en: Taken together with the two previous parts in this series, these findings point to a broader issue in modern work environments.
sentences.zh: 与本系列的前两部分结合起来，这些发现指出了现代工作环境中更广泛的问题。

sentences.en: Namely that the integrity of information becomes a primary security concern in systems that integrate LLMs as part of their operating workflows.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，信息的完整性成为将法学硕士集成为其操作工作流程一部分的系统中的主要安全问题。

sentences.en: The scenarios presented show that attacker-controlled content can not only influence individual outputs and potentially leak information.
sentences.zh: 所呈现的场景表明，攻击者控制的内容不仅会影响个人输出并可能泄露信息。

sentences.en: The attacks themselves can also be replicated and self-propagate through normal user workflows.
sentences.zh: 攻击本身也可以通过正常的用户工作流程进行复制和自我传播。

blocks.html_en: This introduces challenges that extend well beyond initial exploitation. Once malicious instructions are embedded in generated content, they may persist across documents, be redistributed by legitimate users, and be reintroduced into new contexts. At that point, the attack is no longer dependent on its original entry point. It has instead become part of the system’s internal information flow.

sentences.en: This introduces challenges that extend well beyond initial exploitation.
sentences.zh: 这带来的挑战远远超出了最初的利用范围。

sentences.en: Once malicious instructions are embedded in generated content, they may persist across documents, be redistributed by legitimate users, and be reintroduced into new contexts.
sentences.zh: 一旦恶意指令嵌入到生成的内容中，它们可能会在文档中持续存在，被合法用户重新分发，并被重新引入到新的上下文中。

sentences.en: At that point, the attack is no longer dependent on its original entry point.
sentences.zh: 那时，攻击不再依赖于其原始入口点。

sentences.en: It has instead become part of the system’s internal information flow.
sentences.zh: 相反，它已成为系统内部信息流的一部分。

blocks.html_en: A related implication is the loss of traceability. Since affected content is generated and modified through legitimate workflows, the origin of the manipulation becomes difficult to identify after the fact. This complicates both detection and response, particularly in environments where such content is widely shared.

sentences.en: A related implication is the loss of traceability.
sentences.zh: 一个相关的影响是可追溯性的丧失。

sentences.en: Since affected content is generated and modified through legitimate workflows, the origin of the manipulation becomes difficult to identify after the fact.
sentences.zh: 由于受影响的内容是通过合法的工作流程生成和修改的，因此事后很难识别操纵的来源。

sentences.en: This complicates both detection and response, particularly in environments where such content is widely shared.
sentences.zh: 这使得检测和响应变得复杂，特别是在此类内容广泛共享的环境中。

blocks.html_en: Independently of prompt-injection prevention, generated documents should preserve provenance for source material and model-performed edits in metadata. Such controls would not prevent the underlying injection, but they could make traceability much easier.

sentences.en: Independently of prompt-injection prevention, generated documents should preserve provenance for source material and model-performed edits in metadata.
sentences.zh: 独立于即时注入预防，生成的文档应保留元数据中源材料和模型执行编辑的出处。

sentences.en: Such controls would not prevent the underlying injection, but they could make traceability much easier.
sentences.zh: 此类控制不会阻止潜在的注入，但可以使可追溯性变得更加容易。

blocks.html_en: Closing thoughts

sentences.en: Closing thoughts
sentences.zh: 结束语

blocks.html_en: The findings in this series point beyond any single product or implementation. They expose a broader architectural weakness in current LLM-based systems.

sentences.en: The findings in this series point beyond any single product or implementation.
sentences.zh: 本系列的研究结果超出了任何单一产品或实施的范围。

sentences.en: They expose a broader architectural weakness in current LLM-based systems.
sentences.zh: 它们暴露了当前基于法学硕士的系统中更广泛的架构弱点。

blocks.html_en: For AI-assistants to be useful, they often must process emails, documents, webpages, memories, tool outputs, and other information that may be controlled by an attacker. To process that information, it must be included in the model’s context window, where it participates in the same computation as system instructions, user requests, and other trusted information.

sentences.en: For AI-assistants to be useful, they often must process emails, documents, webpages, memories, tool outputs, and other information that may be controlled by an attacker.
sentences.zh: 为了使人工智能助手发挥作用，它们通常必须处理电子邮件、文档、网页、内存、工具输出以及可能由攻击者控制的其他信息。

sentences.en: To process that information, it must be included in the model’s context window, where it participates in the same computation as system instructions, user requests, and other trusted information.
sentences.zh: 要处理该信息，它必须包含在模型的上下文窗口中，在该窗口中它与系统指令、用户请求和其他可信信息参与相同的计算。

blocks.html_en: This creates a fundamental problem: the LLM must process external content to determine what it means, whether it is relevant, and whether it contains an attack. But by the time it makes that determination, the attacker-controlled tokens are already influencing the computation that produces it. The content being inspected participates in the act of inspection. Relying on the model to detect XPIAs therefore resembles asking an interpreter to execute an untrusted program to determine whether that program is safe to execute.

sentences.en: This creates a fundamental problem: the LLM must process external content to determine what it means, whether it is relevant, and whether it contains an attack.
sentences.zh: 这就产生了一个根本问题：法学硕士必须处理外部内容以确定其含义、是否相关以及是否包含攻击。

sentences.en: But by the time it makes that determination, the attacker-controlled tokens are already influencing the computation that produces it.
sentences.zh: 但当它做出决定时，攻击者控制的令牌已经影响了产生该决定的计算。

sentences.en: The content being inspected participates in the act of inspection.
sentences.zh: 被检查的内容参与检查行为。

sentences.en: Relying on the model to detect XPIAs therefore resembles asking an interpreter to execute an untrusted program to determine whether that program is safe to execute.
sentences.zh: 因此，依靠模型来检测 XPIA 类似于要求解释器执行不受信任的程序来确定该程序是否可以安全执行。

blocks.html_en: Detecting and removing malicious content before it reaches the target model merely moves the same problem outward.

sentences.en: Detecting and removing malicious content before it reaches the target model merely moves the same problem outward.
sentences.zh: 在恶意内容到达目标模型之前检测并删除它只会将相同的问题向外转移。

blocks.html_en: Because LLMs can recover semantics across radically different representations, an effective detector must possess comparable semantic recovery capabilities. A detector weaker than the target LLM will cover a smaller representational space, leaving malicious formulations that the target understands but the detector fails to recognize.

sentences.en: Because LLMs can recover semantics across radically different representations, an effective detector must possess comparable semantic recovery capabilities.
sentences.zh: 由于 LLM 可以跨完全不同的表示恢复语义，因此有效的检测器必须具有可比的语义恢复能力。

sentences.en: A detector weaker than the target LLM will cover a smaller representational space, leaving malicious formulations that the target understands but the detector fails to recognize.
sentences.zh: 比目标 LLM 弱的检测器将覆盖较小的表示空间，留下目标可以理解但检测器无法识别的恶意表述。

blocks.html_en: The only generally available technology with comparable semantic capabilities is another LLM. Placing one model in front of another may reduce the success rate of particular attacks, but it creates an “LLMs all the way down” problem, where every LLM introduced to protect another LLM must itself be protected.

sentences.en: The only generally available technology with comparable semantic capabilities is another LLM.
sentences.zh: 唯一具有可比语义能力的通用技术是另一项法学硕士。

sentences.en: Placing one model in front of another may reduce the success rate of particular attacks, but it creates an “LLMs all the way down” problem, where every LLM introduced to protect another LLM must itself be protected.
sentences.zh: 将一个模型放在另一个模型前面可能会降低特定攻击的成功率，但它会产生“LLM 一直向下”的问题，其中为保护另一个 LLM 而引入的每个 LLM 本身都必须受到保护。

blocks.html_en: The long-term challenge likely lies in designing systems in which goals and intentions also exist independently of the information being processed. Current LLM architectures provide no reliable separation between intention and interpretation. Thus, in current systems with embedded LLMs, attacker-controlled information can influence not only what the model produces, but what the model believes it has been asked to produce.

sentences.en: The long-term challenge likely lies in designing systems in which goals and intentions also exist independently of the information being processed.
sentences.zh: 长期的挑战可能在于设计系统，其中目标和意图也独立于正在处理的信息而存在。

sentences.en: Current LLM architectures provide no reliable separation between intention and interpretation.
sentences.zh: 当前的法学硕士架构没有提供意图和解释之间的可靠分离。

sentences.en: Thus, in current systems with embedded LLMs, attacker-controlled information can influence not only what the model produces, but what the model believes it has been asked to produce.
sentences.zh: 因此，在当前具有嵌入式 LLM 的系统中，攻击者控制的信息不仅会影响模型生成的内容，还会影响模型认为已被要求生成的内容。

blocks.html_en: For that reason, any system that integrates an LLM into a trusted workflow today must assume that attacker-controlled content entering the model’s context will result in compromise at some rate.

sentences.en: For that reason, any system that integrates an LLM into a trusted workflow today must assume that attacker-controlled content entering the model’s context will result in compromise at some rate.

content_html_zh:
我要感谢 Microsoft 产品团队和 Microsoft 安全响应中心 (MSRC) 在技术分析和已披露漏洞的缓解方面与我合作。 下面反映的编辑意见仅代表作者的观点，并不一定反映与我合作的组织的观点。

概括

本文中描述的调查结果是与 MSRC 和 Microsoft 产品团队协调披露的一部分。 向 Microsoft 提供了重现步骤、视频、环境假设以及测试期间使用的确切概念验证 (PoC) 提示。 他们还被告知披露前有 90 天的协调期。 该期限曾两次延长，协调期为 144 天。

在本系列的第 1 部分和第 2 部分中，我展示了外部输入如何影响 Copilot 响应，并且在某些情况下，可能通过跨域提示注入攻击 (XPIA) 导致机密性影响。 本报告以这些发现为基础，并将 XPIA 分析从单交互妥协扩展到跨可信文档工作流程的传播。 它表明，一份文档中攻击者控制的指令可以复制到 Copilot 生成或 Copilot 编辑的 Word 文档中，从而导致这些下游文档成为同一攻击的新载体。

之前存在人工智能蠕虫的例子。 值得注意的是，Morris II 在 GenAI 驱动的电子邮件助理生态系统中展示了自我复制的即时传播。 然而，据我所知，这是文档传播的人工智能蠕虫通过主流商业生产力套件中的正常工作流程进行自我传播的首次公开演示。

报告的场景是：

  1. 隐藏在外部共享文档中的恶意指令可能会使 Copilot 更改 Word 中起草或编辑的文档，并将攻击传播到新文档。

完整攻击简介

袭击

攻击者将隐藏指令放入文档中，该文档随后用作 Copilot for Word 中的源材料。 Copilot 可能会将这些指令解释为用户请求的一部分，从而导致其操纵正在起草或编辑的文档。 然后，副驾驶也可以将隐藏的指令复制到生成的文档中，将该文档变成新的载体。 如果载体随后在另一个 Copilot 辅助工作流程中使用，则即使攻击者的原始文档不存在，指令也可以再次触发并传播到更多文档中。

例子

考虑一名准备财务报告的员工。 员工从已被泄露的受信任网站下载市场分析，但不知道该文件包含隐藏指令。 然后，员工在与 Copilot 一起起草报告时将分析结果作为源材料包含在内。 隐藏的指令导致 Copilot 更改财务报告中的内部数据并将攻击复制到新文档中。 员工在内部保存并共享看似合法的报告。 后来，一位同事将其用作另一份报告的源材料；指令再次触发，更改新报告，并向前复制。 因此，攻击可以继续进行，而无需受感染网站或原始恶意文档的进一步参与。 随着受影响的报告被重复使用，其他报告和文档可能成为攻击的载体。

发布时的披露状态

  • 供应商： 微软
  • 协调披露：通过 MSRC 和 Microsoft 产品团队处理
  • 本文包含：Microsoft Copilot for Word 中的 XPIA 和自传播场景
  • 客户行动：截至发布时，尚未有任何客户端补救措施能够完全解决该问题。 客户可以通过以下方式减少暴露：与 Copilot 一起使用时，将外部来源的文档视为不可信。在开始 Copilot 生成或编辑之前查看任何附加文档。在重复使用、共享或分发 Copilot 生成或 Copilot 编辑的文档之前，仔细查看它们。

威胁模型

攻击者不需要访问受害者的 Microsoft 365 租户。 攻击者只需与受害者共享恶意文档即可。 这可以通过 SharePoint、Teams、Outlook 或任何其他共享文档的方式来完成。

安全边界和观察到的行为

这种情况下的相关安全边界是附加文档和当前起草文档之间的边界。 如果任何附加文档包含 XPIA，则可能会触发攻击。

副驾驶必须阅读所有附加文件，以确定当前起草任务中应包含哪些部分。 但是，附加文档应被视为不受信任的信息，而不是受信任的用户指令。

边界违规 通过电子邮件/共享点/其他共享选项下载或共享攻击者控制的文档。 如果在起草任务期间将此类文件附加给 Copilot，信任就会被破坏。

预期行为 当用户要求 Copilot 起草例如基于所附文件的第一季度财务报告，Copilot 应利用所附文件中的信息，而不应将文件中嵌入的指示视为权威指示。

观察到的行为 文档中嵌入的说明会导致 Copilot 改变其行为。 这里呈现为： 1：Copilot 默默地更改财务报告中的数值 2：Copilot 通过粘贴到下游文档中传播完整的 XPIA，然后可以在以后的起草会议中将其用作附件\

跨越 Word 中的信任边界

这些场景的初始攻击媒介使用恶意文档。 恶意文档包含 JSON 格式的恶意提示，当该文档包含在 Copilot 的上下文中时，该提示会触发攻击。 该提示可以呈现为白色背景上的白色文本并以较小的字体大小来隐藏它，以防止受害者发现。 由于 Copilot for Word 在将文本传递到底层大语言模型 (LLM) 之前会删除所有文本格式（例如颜色和字体大小），因此即使受害者看不到该文本，Copilot 仍然可以完全读取该文本。 通过将攻击嵌入到具有任务相关文本的看似良性的文档中，可以进一步隐藏攻击。

此攻击需要将恶意文档作为 Copilot 上下文的一部分包含在 Word 中。 因此，根据所使用的 Copilot 版本，受害者必须：

  1. 在 Copilot for Word 中主动附加或上传文档。
  2. 在工作/工作 IQ 模式下使用“使用 Copilot 编辑”功能，让 Copilot 在受害者的 OneDrive 中找到恶意文档。 在这种情况下，Copilot 必须认为该文档相关并将其包含在上下文中。 因此，攻击者需要制作一份文档来增加其中之一或两者的可能性。

该漏洞与 Word 中的“魔笔”和“使用 Copilot 编辑”功能相关。

攻击分两个阶段发生。 第一阶段建立立足点，在第二阶段，攻击在使用 Copilot for Word 作为起草或编辑部分的文档中自我传播。

Stage 1:

在第一阶段，攻击者制作了一个包含恶意隐藏提示的文档。 在我最初的 PoC 中，我使用的文档仅包含白色背景上的白色文本的恶意提示。 这样做是为了说明恶意文档不需要与受害者的任务相关，Copilot 就可以使用它。 如果它包含在上下文中，则会被读取，因此可能会触发攻击。

PoC 提示分为两部分：

  • 第一部分包含有关如何影响文档的说明。 这可能包括从摘要含义的轻微改变到财务文件中数字的改变。 关键是以一种让副驾驶相信它与任务相关且良性的方式制定提示。 在我的许多实验中，我实际上还需要指示 Copilot 突出显示它所做的更改，因为它们通常是难以发现的有意义的更改。 这表明攻击以有意义的方式巧妙地改变文本是多么有效，即使是细心的审阅者也很容易逃脱。 在现实环境中，攻击者显然不会包含此类指令。 因此，对于本披露的其余部分，我将在财务报告中使用更改数字，因为这是一个立即可见的变化。
  • 第二部分包含自我传播攻击的指令。 确切的措辞在这里也很重要，但它通常被认为是为了跟踪下游文件中的来源。 它还包含有关如何隐藏自身的说明，这些说明被框定为提高可读性的说明。

值得注意的是，这个新的攻击媒介现在是一个内部创建的文档，并具有随之而来的所有信任。 因此，受害者只需与同事共享此文档即可传播攻击。 如果受害者或同事在起草或编辑时使用受影响的文档作为 Copilot for Word 的附件，攻击就会蔓延到这些新文档。

在所有报告的 PoC 场景中，Copilot 都会更改生成或编辑的文档，并将隐藏指令复制到这些文档中。 当这些文档本身被用作新下游文档的上下文的一部分时，攻击再次触发。 请注意，在第二阶段，原始攻击文档不再是新下游文档附件的一部分，但攻击也触发并传播到这些文档。

影响

由于攻击能够通过内部文档传播，一旦超出其初始入口点，攻击的追踪就变得极其困难。 由于每个文档都是由合法的内部资源创建的，并且 Copilot 的编辑在获得受害者批准后不会可见，这进一步加剧了这种情况。 更广泛的担忧是，如果攻击通过普通文档工作流程在组织内悄然传播，则可能会侵蚀组织做出决策的信息基础。

此外，不知道自己受到攻击影响的组织也可能通过共享 Microsoft SharePoint 网站或共享 Microsoft Teams 上的协作将其传播到其他组织。 因此，特定组织的初始攻击向量实际上可能来自已经受到影响的可信合作伙伴。 这再次增加了受害者在起草过程中选择将受影响的文档包含在 Copilot for Word 上下文中的可能性。

最近，Copilot 还与 Microsoft Cowork 或 Microsoft Scout 等系统更加深入地集成，将助手扩展到文档、工具和协作工作流程的自动操作和创建。 在此类系统中，此处描述的问题的实际影响可能会迅速扩大。 基本机制保持不变，但它可以传播或影响的潜在表面以机器速度扩展。

减轻漏洞

Microsoft 成功缓解了最初提交的 PoC 提示，并在本披露过程中部署了多个修复程序。 其中每一个都通过关闭报告的特定有效负载来提高标准，并且随后重现行为需要更改有效负载，而不是直接重用旧的有效负载。

然而，原始报告还描述了更广泛的漏洞类别，其中源文档中嵌入的指令可能会影响 Copilot 的生成并将其自身复制到下游文档中。 更改请求的操作或措辞会更改有效负载，但不会更改底层漏洞或传播机制。 使用修改后的有效负载，可以重现完整的攻击链并部署所有缓解措施（本报告中的 PoC 就是这样一个案例）。 因此，该漏洞类别在发布时仍然可以被利用。

课程尚未完全结束反映了根本问题的严重性。 正如最后的想法所讨论的，该弱点是架构性的，并且在当前基于法学硕士的系统中是共有的。 我不知道目前任何同类产品中是否有完全缓解此类问题的方法。 完全解决这个问题需要研究而不是单一补丁。 在这些限制内，微软的修复有意义地减少了暴露，并且第 1 部分和第 2 部分中涵盖的内存和电子邮件正文向量得到了彻底缓解。 我要感谢微软为解决一个真正困难的问题所做的持续和实质性的努力。

影响

与本系列的前两部分结合起来，这些发现指出了现代工作环境中更广泛的问题。 也就是说，信息的完整性成为将法学硕士集成为其操作工作流程一部分的系统中的主要安全问题。 所呈现的场景表明，攻击者控制的内容不仅会影响个人输出并可能泄露信息。 攻击本身也可以通过正常的用户工作流程进行复制和自我传播。

这带来的挑战远远超出了最初的利用范围。 一旦恶意指令嵌入到生成的内容中，它们可能会在文档中持续存在，被合法用户重新分发，并被重新引入到新的上下文中。 那时，攻击不再依赖于其原始入口点。 相反，它已成为系统内部信息流的一部分。

一个相关的影响是可追溯性的丧失。 由于受影响的内容是通过合法的工作流程生成和修改的，因此事后很难识别操纵的来源。 这使得检测和响应变得复杂，特别是在此类内容广泛共享的环境中。

独立于即时注入预防，生成的文档应保留元数据中源材料和模型执行编辑的出处。 此类控制不会阻止潜在的注入，但可以使可追溯性变得更加容易。

结束语

本系列的研究结果超出了任何单一产品或实施的范围。 它们暴露了当前基于法学硕士的系统中更广泛的架构弱点。

为了使人工智能助手发挥作用，它们通常必须处理电子邮件、文档、网页、内存、工具输出以及可能由攻击者控制的其他信息。 要处理该信息，它必须包含在模型的上下文窗口中，在该窗口中它与系统指令、用户请求和其他可信信息参与相同的计算。

这就产生了一个根本问题：法学硕士必须处理外部内容以确定其含义、是否相关以及是否包含攻击。 但当它做出决定时，攻击者控制的令牌已经影响了产生该决定的计算。 被检查的内容参与检查行为。 因此，依靠模型来检测 XPIA 类似于要求解释器执行不受信任的程序来确定该程序是否可以安全执行。

在恶意内容到达目标模型之前检测并删除它只会将相同的问题向外转移。

由于 LLM 可以跨完全不同的表示恢复语义，因此有效的检测器必须具有可比的语义恢复能力。 比目标 LLM 弱的检测器将覆盖较小的表示空间，留下目标可以理解但检测器无法识别的恶意表述。

唯一具有可比语义能力的通用技术是另一项法学硕士。 将一个模型放在另一个模型前面可能会降低特定攻击的成功率，但它会产生“LLM 一直向下”的问题，其中为保护另一个 LLM 而引入的每个 LLM 本身都必须受到保护。

长期的挑战可能在于设计系统，其中目标和意图也独立于正在处理的信息而存在。 当前的法学硕士架构没有提供意图和解释之间的可靠分离。 因此，在当前具有嵌入式 LLM 的系统中，攻击者控制的信息不仅会影响模型生成的内容，还会影响模型认为已被要求生成的内容。

因此，当今将 LLM 集成到可信工作流程中的任何系统都必须假设进入模型上下文的攻击者控制的内容将在某种程度上导致妥协。
